A financial analyst agent can produce a number that matches a filing perfectly and still be wrong. The value is right, but it belongs to a different entity, concept, period, unit, or scope. A reference-answer check marks that answer wrong — and then stops, because the grader cannot say why.

**NumTrace** (arXiv:2610.34887) is built to say why. It audits the provenance of each numerical claim a financial analyst agent makes — its source document and its financial semantics — across **540 questions over 2,163 SEC EDGAR documents**. The reference answers are built on a frozen snapshot of those filings, following accounting rules rather than scraped numbers.

## Three Verdicts Instead of One

Each claim gets three independent verdicts: **value**, **binding**, and **support**. Keeping value and binding separate is the point of the design, because it makes a specific error class visible — **right number, wrong account** (RNWA). A claim has an RNWA error when it passes the value check but fails the binding check. The RNWA rate is simply the gap between value-only pass rate and joint value-and-binding pass rate.

The benchmark also claims a first: it is the first numerical benchmark covering who holds a company's shares (**Form 13F**) and what its executives are owed (**Item 402(i)**).

## The Agents Fail in a Consistent Way

The audit covers Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. **RNWA errors make up 67.5–81.8% of each agent's failing claims.** The failures are not arithmetic noise or hallucinated figures — they are figures that are real, correctly retrieved, and attached to the wrong thing.

The 13F co-filing group questions are the sharpest illustration. About **91% of claims pass the value check, but fewer than half pass the binding check**. The agent finds the number, and then attaches it to the wrong filer in a group of co-filers — a distinction that only matters to someone who understands the filing structure, and that most readers will not catch.

## Why This Matters Beyond Finance

The pattern generalises. Any domain where a retrieved value must be bound to a specific entity-property-period tuple produces this failure shape: medical coding, contract term extraction, supply chain records, regulatory reporting. The value is right and the binding is wrong, so the output reads as confident and is wrong in a way that reference keys cannot diagnose.

Two practical consequences follow. First, for anyone deploying analyst agents, value-only validation is close to worthless — it would let through two-thirds to four-fifths of the agents' errors. Second, for the benchmark and eval community, NumTrace suggests a general template: split the verdict, so the grader can distinguish retrieval failure from binding failure and report the second separately.
